prompt.context: Six months out of HBS, a frustrated classmate calls you to complain that the fast food burger joint that he bought has been steadily losing money for the last 3 months. He wants to know what you think he should do about it.
prompt.question: Where do you start? What would you do to help your classmate understand and address the situation?

clarifying_info.q: What do you mean by losing money — have profits declined or is the business actually in the red?
Have revenues decreased, costs increased, or both?
Are there fewer customers, or are existing customers spending less per visit?
Is the issue primarily internal or external?
clarifying_info.a: The issue is external — a new competitor opened across the street.

clarifying_info.q: What does the new competitor offer?
clarifying_info.a: They serve chicken dinners and appear to offer a completely different experience.

framework: Define what 'losing money' means: profit decline vs. operating at a loss
Diagnose the revenue side: fewer customers or lower spend per visit
Diagnose the cost side: have costs risen independently of revenue?
Identify external factors: new competition, economic changes, demographic shifts in the area
Identify internal factors: food quality, pricing, major events (health code violations, illness)
Assess the competitor's value proposition through first-hand visits and primary research
Generate and prioritize options to recover traffic, evaluating ROI and speed of impact
Develop an action plan with timing and accountabilities

questions.prompt: What clarifying questions should you ask up front to frame the analysis?
questions.guidance: Strong answers immediately probe both sides of the P&L. Key questions: (1) Have revenues decreased, costs increased, or both? (2) Is the business in the red or just less profitable? (3) Was it profitable 3 months ago — what changed? (4) Are there fewer customers or is spend per customer down? (5) Is there new competition? (6) Has there been a local economic change or a major negative event (illness, health code violation)?

questions.prompt: Given that revenues have fallen due to fewer customers, walk through the possible causes — both external and internal.
questions.guidance: External: new competition offering better value, shift in consumer eating habits, local business closure reducing foot traffic, economic downturn in the area. Internal: deteriorating food quality, price increases, poor service, negative event such as a health-code violation or customer illness. A strong candidate structures these as a MECE list and then asks which bucket the interviewer wants to focus on.

questions.prompt: A new chicken restaurant opened across the street. How would you assess their value proposition and understand what is driving customers away?
questions.guidance: First-hand visit to the competitor: evaluate food quality, pricing, menu variety (healthier options), service speed, cleanliness, facility layout, parking, and accessibility. Then conduct the same audit of the burger joint. Follow up with primary research: customer intercept interviews at both locations, asking customers to rate food and experience, identifying overlap (former burger customers now exclusively at chicken place vs. dual visitors vs. entirely new customers). The goal is to isolate the specific value gaps.

questions.prompt: Based on your research findings, how would you develop and prioritize options to recover traffic?
questions.guidance: Generate improvement options across: menu innovation (new items, healthier choices), facility renovation, taste/quality improvements, pricing adjustments, marketing and promotions, and service upgrades. Evaluate each option on two criteria: (1) speed to drive traffic back and (2) return on investment. Prioritize the highest-impact, fastest options and build a sequenced action plan with clear owners and timelines. Acknowledge that a financial analysis may also be needed to decide whether improvement is viable vs. closing or selling.

brainstorming.prompt: What are all the possible reasons a fast food restaurant could see a decline in customer traffic?

categories.name: External — Competition
ideas: New direct competitor opened nearby
Existing competitor launched promotions or improved menu
New category competitor offering a different experience (e.g., fast-casual, chicken vs. burger)

categories.name: External — Market/Environment
ideas: Local economic downturn reducing discretionary spending
Major employer or office building nearby closed, reducing lunch traffic
Demographic shift in the neighborhood
Road construction reducing accessibility or parking

categories.name: External — Consumer Trends
ideas: Shift toward healthier eating reducing burger demand
Increased delivery/meal-kit competition
Changing dietary preferences (vegetarian, low-carb)

categories.name: Internal — Product
ideas: Decline in food quality or consistency
Menu too limited or outdated
Portion sizes reduced
Price increases not matched by perceived value

categories.name: Internal — Operations
ideas: Slower service or longer wait times
Cleanliness issues
Poor staff attitude or turnover
Reduced operating hours

categories.name: Internal — Events
ideas: Health code violation or public notice
Reported case of food-borne illness
Negative online reviews or social media incident

recommendation: Conduct immediate first-hand competitive audit of the new chicken restaurant and the burger joint on all key value dimensions (food quality, price, variety, service, facility)
Run customer intercept interviews at both locations to quantify the overlap in customer bases and identify specific value gaps driving the switch
Prioritize 2-3 highest-ROI improvements — likely menu diversification and quality upgrades — and launch them within 60 days
Assess the financial viability of the turnaround: if required investment exceeds the net present value of recoverable profit, consider selling or repurposing the location
risks: Turnaround investment may not be recoverable if the competitive disadvantage is structural (location, brand, category preference)
Attempting too many changes simultaneously can confuse existing loyal customers
Delayed action allows the competitor to deepen its customer relationships further
next_steps: Visit competitor and conduct side-by-side audit within one week
Design and execute customer survey/intercept study within two weeks
Analyze survey data and build a prioritized options matrix with cost and revenue-impact estimates
Present recommendation to classmate with go/no-go criteria for investment vs. exit
